edition.deck: New evidence sharpens questions over Spain’s rail disaster, while investigations and policy disputes unfold across the UK and Denmark.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and substantial new reporting from the day. Returning stories appear only where the gather adds a significant development, fresh evidence or a distinct angle.

content.headline: Spain train-crash recordings appear to show clearance given despite a stalled
content.shortHeadline: Spain crash audio raises questions over control-centre decisions
content.standfirst: Recordings published in Spanish media appear to capture a controller authorising a train to continue at normal speed while another remained stopped. The death toll has reached 69; investigators have yet to establish the full sequence of failures.

image.caption: Investigators inspect debris at the crash site near Toledo.

sources.originalTitle: Audio reveals exchanges between control centre and drivers before deadly Spain train crash
Spain begins mourning period as search continues for train crash victims
Hvordan endte to højhastighedstog med at køre sammen i Spanien?
How did the Spain train crash happen and what will investigators be asking?
Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain
Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network

segments.body: Recordings of conversations between train drivers and a Madrid control centre appear to show a Renfe train being told to continue at normal speed after a signalling failure, while an Iryo train ahead was still stationary. At least 69 people died when the Renfe train struck it near Urda.

segments.title: What remains unclear
segments.body: The recordings are evidence, not a final account of the disaster. Authorities are investigating the signalling failure and the decisions that followed; Spain’s transport minister has called the instruction to resume at normal speed inexplicable. The Iryo driver appears to have told the control centre the train could not move.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s rail analysis says investigators will need to establish both what caused the signalling failure and why one train was authorised to proceed while the other remained stopped. The audio does not answer those technical questions.

segments.title: Safety under scrutiny
segments.body: Spain is mourning the victims, while rail drivers have gone ahead with a planned strike over safety. The crash has intensified questions about the country’s high-speed network, coming nine months after another fatal collision on the same route. The investigation has not established whether the two disasters share a cause.

content.headline: Russian drone strike on Dnipro railway station kills at least 14, officials say
content.shortHeadline: At least 14 killed in strike on Dnipro railway station
content.standfirst: A drone hit a crowded platform in the central Ukrainian city, according to local officials. The attack also wounded at least 14 people, including a child; Russia’s military has not publicly commented.

image.caption: A blast-damaged train near the site of the strike in Dnipro.

sources.originalTitle: Russian drone attack on Ukrainian train station kills at least 14, officials say

segments.body: At least 14 people were killed and 14 wounded when a Russian jet-powered drone struck a crowded platform at Dnipro’s main railway station, regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said. A passenger train bound for Zaporizhzhia was at a platform when the drone hit, Ukraine’s state railway operator said.

segments.title: Other strikes
segments.body: Officials also reported deaths and injuries after attacks in Chernihiv and Kremenchuk. A day of mourning has been declared for Dnipro and Chernihiv. Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukraine’s rail network, but denies deliberately targeting civilians; its military had not publicly commented on the Dnipro strike in the reporting gathered here.

content.headline: Xi’s party expels 33 members as discipline dominates China’s political gathering
content.shortHeadline: China expels 33 party members in record purge
content.standfirst: The Communist Party’s latest plenum ended with a record number of expulsions, including 16 military members. Observers say Xi Jinping’s anti-corruption drive is increasingly tied to loyalty and control; the specific charges remain unclear.

image.caption: Empty seats at the Communist Party gathering in Beijing.

sources.originalTitle: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering

segments.body: China’s Communist Party expelled 33 members as its four-day plenum ended, the highest number reported at such a gathering. Sixteen were from the military. The party cited “serious disciplinary and legal violations” but gave no specific charges; attendance was also unusually low, with 279 members present.

segments.title: Discipline and power
segments.body: Analyst Chong Ja Ian told the BBC the campaign has become “an effort to consolidate and maintain authority”, rather than simply to address corruption. The expulsions add to a record 51 members removed during Xi’s third term. Observers say the scale of the military purge raises questions about leadership and readiness.

The gathering comes ahead of the Communist Party Congress scheduled for 2027, when the party is due to choose its next leader. Analysts expect Xi to retain a central role in selecting personnel, but the reporting also raises a longer-term question: whether concentrating power around one leader could create a succession problem.

content.headline: Alaska governor orders probe into alleged same-name candidate scheme
content.shortHeadline: Alaska orders investigation into alleged spoiler-candidate scheme
content.standfirst: Governor Mike Dunleavy has ordered a probe after a report alleged Democratic-linked operatives tried to recruit candidates with the same name as Republican senator Dan Sullivan. The campaign denies wrongdoing; whether any law was broken remains unresolved.

image.caption: Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into the allegations.

sources.originalTitle: Alaska governor orders probe into Democratic campaign's alleged links to same-name candidate

segments.body: Alaska’s Republican governor has ordered the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether a reported effort to recruit candidates with the same name as incumbent senator Dan Sullivan violated state law. The New York Times reported that people connected to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign and party officials sought to recruit a second Dan Sullivan. Peltola’s campaign denies involvement.

segments.title: A dispute without a finding
segments.body: The second Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher, has denied links to Peltola’s campaign. Alaska’s Supreme Court previously allowed him to remain on the ballot, and election-law experts told the BBC that persuading someone to run is not itself a crime. The governor has not specified which laws might have been broken; the investigation has not reached a finding.

content.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro says he will lead Brazil’s opposition from the US
content.shortHeadline: Flávio Bolsonaro claims role as Brazil’s opposition leader
content.standfirst: After leaving Brazil following his election defeat, Bolsonaro says he will lead the opposition from the United States and alleges fraud without providing evidence. Brazil’s electoral authority says the vote followed the law.

image.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro arrived in Florida after leaving Brazil.

sources.originalTitle: Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself 'leader of Brazil' after election loss

segments.body: Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has called himself “leader of Brazil” in a letter posted on social media, saying he will lead the opposition from the United States. He has not conceded his loss to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who won by 4.4 million votes.

segments.title: Fraud claim rejected
segments.body: Bolsonaro alleges electoral fraud but provides no evidence in the letter. Brazil’s electoral authority says the vote was conducted according to the law, and an analysis by BBC Brazil and BBC Verify found the extended polling hours affected far fewer voters than the margin of victory. Bolsonaro left Brazil after failing to comply with an order to surrender his passports as part of a money-laundering investigation; he has not been charged in that probe and denies wrongdoing.

content.headline: Google’s Finnish datacentre project faces criminal investigation over forest
content.shortHeadline: Finland investigates Google subsidiary over forest clearing
content.standfirst: Police are examining whether a Google subsidiary breached environmental rules by clearing and draining forest before required assessments were complete. Work at two sites has already been ordered to stop; the company says it acted on its understanding of the law.

image.caption: Cleared land at the planned Google datacentre site in Muhos, Finland.

sources.originalTitle: Finland launches criminal investigation into Google’s clearing of forest for datacentre site

segments.body: Finnish police have opened a criminal investigation into possible environmental-law breaches at a planned Google datacentre site in Muhos. Authorities allege that Tuike Finland, a Google subsidiary, cleared and drained 330 hectares of forest before completing legally required environmental impact assessments.

segments.title: Wider scrutiny
segments.body: Finnish authorities ordered Google to suspend work at Muhos and Otanmäki earlier this month. The company’s Finland manager apologised for the clearances but said the company acted according to its understanding of the legislation at the time. The investigation will examine, among other issues, drainage and water management; no finding of criminal liability is reported.

The case is part of a wider debate in Finland about the environmental and economic effects of datacentre investment. Authorities are considering 145 proposed datacentres. A petition calling for tighter regulation and compensation has attracted more than 93,000 signatures; experts quoted in the reporting question how much local benefit the projects bring.

content.headline: Medical micro-robots move closer to targeted drug delivery
content.shortHeadline: Micro-robots could deliver drugs more precisely inside the body
content.standfirst: Researchers are developing magnetically guided devices to deliver treatment in the gut and, eventually, blood vessels. Some approaches have worked in animals or models, but the more advanced technology is not yet ready for use in patients.

image.caption: Illustration of a micro-robot designed to deliver medicine in the gut.

sources.originalTitle: The astonishing micro-robots you swallow that spot cancer and might help treat it

segments.body: A swallowable camera capsule is already used by NHS doctors to investigate gut problems. Researchers are now developing smaller, steerable devices that could deliver medicines to specific locations. A team in Beijing reported using a 6.5mm robot to deliver insulin to the lower intestine of pigs; this is not evidence of a treatment ready for patients.

segments.title: From gut to bloodstream
segments.body: Researchers are testing magnetic control to guide devices through the body. A team at ETH Zürich has steered a 2mm robot through a pig’s bloodstream, while a separate test used a silicone model of brain circulation to demonstrate delivery of a clot-dissolving drug. Devices small enough to move through blood vessels are still at an early stage.

The proposed benefit is more precise delivery, potentially allowing a lower dose and reducing the risk of toxicity. Researchers also describe possible applications in tumours and aneurysms, but these remain research aims. The reporting suggests that use in patients of the more advanced devices is likely to be at least a decade away.

content.headline: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal
content.shortHeadline: DoorDash agrees to buy Instacart for $17bn
content.standfirst: The companies say the deal would widen grocery and delivery options, while expanding DoorDash beyond restaurant meals. The merger is expected to take about a year and may face scrutiny from competition regulators.

image.caption: DoorDash and Instacart have agreed to combine their delivery businesses.

sources.originalTitle: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand customer options

segments.body: DoorDash has agreed to acquire grocery-delivery company Instacart in a deal valued at $17bn. The companies say Instacart customers would gain access to 150,000 stores, up from 100,000, and DoorDash would expand further into retail. They expect to continue operating independently until the transaction is completed.

segments.title: Regulatory questions
segments.body: The transaction is expected to take about a year to complete and would be DoorDash’s largest acquisition to date. Reuters reported the merger may raise antitrust concerns. New York City’s consumer and worker-protection commission criticised the proposed consolidation and said it would continue enforcing delivery workers’ rights.

content.headline: MPs ask watchdog to investigate possible leak before Healey’s Budget
content.shortHeadline: Watchdog asked to investigate market-sensitive Budget leak
content.standfirst: The Treasury select committee chair has asked the FCA and Treasury to examine whether information about a temporary bank-tax rise reached markets before the Budget. The reported leak moved bank share prices; no finding of improper disclosure has been made.

image.caption: John Healey delivers his Budget statement in the House of Commons.

sources.originalTitle: John Healey faces questions over budget leak that moved bank share prices

segments.body: Meg Hillier, chair of the Commons Treasury select committee, has asked the Financial Conduct Authority and the Treasury to investigate a Bloomberg report published more than an hour before John Healey’s Budget. It said the bank surcharge would rise by less than lenders had feared and would be temporary; bank share prices moved after publication.

segments.title: What investigators are being asked to establish
segments.body: Hillier wants the Treasury to say how many people had access to the information and whether banks or their representatives were briefed before the Budget. She asked the FCA whether the disclosure could amount to improper release of inside information and what effect it had on securities. The committee is due to question Healey next month.

content.headline: IFS warns Healey’s Budget leaves a £28bn spending challenge
content.shortHeadline: IFS warns next year’s spending review could mean real-terms cuts
content.standfirst: The Institute for Fiscal Studies says the Budget leaves a funding gap for public services and defence, with decisions deferred until next year. It warns some departments could face real-terms cuts or further tax speculation.

image.caption: The IFS says some public services could face real-terms cuts in the next spending review.

sources.originalTitle: Healey’s budget paves way for ‘brutal’ spending review next year, warns IFS

segments.body: The Institute for Fiscal Studies says John Healey’s Budget left a £28bn shortfall in the public finances that must be addressed to avoid renewed austerity. Its director, Helen Miller, said existing plans could require an extra £17bn for unprotected departments in 2030–31, before another £11bn needed for the commitment to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP.

segments.title: Decisions deferred
segments.body: The IFS says departmental spending plans remain broadly unchanged in cash terms, which could mean real-terms cuts as inflation raises the cost of public services. Miller called the decision to defer major choices to next year’s spending review a risk, saying it could bring damaging speculation about tax rises. The government has promised there will be no return to austerity.

content.headline: Healey says welfare spending must fall as watchdog forecasts rise
content.shortHeadline: Healey promises to reduce welfare bill, with reforms still to come
content.standfirst: The chancellor says the benefits bill must come down, particularly through expectations on young people to accept work or training support. He has not set a timetable or target, and says reforms will follow two reviews.

image.caption: John Healey said the government would expect young people to take up offers of support.

sources.originalTitle: Healey vows to cut welfare bill before next election with ‘tough’ approach to young people

segments.body: John Healey has said the government will reduce the benefits bill before the next election, while taking a “tough” approach to young people who do not accept offers of work or training. He described the welfare system as unsustainable but ruled out “crude cuts”; no detailed policy changes or timetable have been set out.

segments.title: Forecasts and unanswered questions
segments.body: The Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts total welfare spending rising from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030, with about a quarter going to sickness and disability benefits. Downing Street later said no arbitrary target or timetable had been set. The government says it will announce changes after reviews of young people and work, and disability benefits.

The Resolution Foundation criticised the Budget as “scattergun” and said its energy support would not prevent bills rising above the levels seen during the 2022–23 energy shock. It forecasts a typical annual bill of £1,750 after support in 2026–27, compared with £1,685 during that earlier surge.

content.headline: Residents evacuated from east London flats over risk of structural collapse
content.shortHeadline: More than 200 homes evacuated over serious structural concerns
content.standfirst: Residents of three Canning Town apartment blocks were told to leave after engineers identified cracks and sagging in supporting transfer slabs. They do not know when they can return, and longer-term accommodation remains a concern.

image.caption: One of the Canning Town apartment blocks evacuated over structural concerns.

sources.originalTitle: I had to flee my £335,000 new-build flat over risk of tower block collapse

segments.body: Residents of more than 200 apartments in three blocks in Canning Town were evacuated after being told that serious structural issues posed a risk to life. The buildings, part of the Royal Gateway development, are less than 10 years old. Some residents learned of the evacuation when police knocked on their doors in the early hours.

segments.title: Support and the cause
segments.body: The managing agent, Prime Property Management, said the concern relates to cracks and sagging in transfer slabs that help support the buildings. It said engineers raised the issue while preparing safety cases and that residents can return only when it is safe. Newham Council said it opened a rest centre and provided emergency accommodation for the night; residents told the i they remain uncertain about longer-term arrangements.

content.headline: UK gambling tax rise targets slot-machine venues as losses mount
content.shortHeadline: Budget raises tax on slot machines as concern grows over losses
content.standfirst: The Budget raises machine games duty from 20% to 25%, aiming to raise nearly £150m a year. The Guardian’s reporting shows how quickly money can be lost in adult gaming centres; the industry says its venues are regulated and offer player-protection measures.

image.caption: Adult gaming centres and bookmakers on a street in Peterborough.

sources.originalTitle: How £100 vanishes in minutes: inside the ‘slot farms’ targeted in the budget

segments.body: Gamblers in Great Britain lost £2.7bn on slot machines last year, according to the Guardian. The Budget raises the tax on machines from 20% to 25%, which the chancellor says will bring in nearly £150m a year. In a test at a Peterborough venue, the newspaper watched £100 disappear in about five minutes.

segments.title: How the venues work
segments.body: Adult gaming centres often stay open around the clock and use snacks, drinks and promotions to keep customers playing, the Guardian reports. Critics say the machines are associated with higher rates of problem gambling and question staff bonuses linked to customer losses. Bacta, the trade body, says its members provide trained staff, self-exclusion and other player-protection tools.

content.headline: HMRC assigns compliance managers to more than 200 UK-linked billionaires
content.shortHeadline: HMRC targets more than 200 billionaires in tax-compliance drive
content.standfirst: The tax authority says it will offer dedicated managers to billionaires with a UK tax footprint and use new technology to identify risks among wealthy taxpayers. It estimates the wider wealthy tax gap at £3.6bn in 2024–25.

image.caption: HMRC is assigning managers to wealthy taxpayers with UK tax obligations.

sources.originalTitle: HMRC puts 200 billionaires on UK tax crackdown hitlist

segments.body: HM Revenue and Customs says more than 200 billionaires with a UK tax footprint will be assigned customer compliance managers. The managers will offer discussions before tax returns are filed, aiming to clarify complex affairs spanning multiple taxes, entities and jurisdictions.

segments.title: Broader enforcement
segments.body: HMRC also plans to use analytics, automated triggers and artificial intelligence to identify risks among people with income above £200,000 or assets over £2m. The authority estimates the wealthy tax gap at £3.6bn in 2024–25 and says its measures will contribute at least £500m towards a wider tax-revenue target. The figures are HMRC estimates, not recovered sums.

content.headline: Russell Brand’s wife gives evidence at his rape and sexual assault trial
content.shortHeadline: Laura Brand testifies as Russell Brand’s trial continues
content.standfirst: Laura Brand told jurors her husband was caring and attentive, while describing an earlier split over his promiscuity. Russell Brand denies seven charges involving six women; the trial is continuing.

image.caption: Russell and Laura Brand arrive at Southwark Crown Court.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
Russell Brand’s wife tells court he is ‘amazingly attentive husband’
From sex ‘obsession’ to losing friends, key takeaways from Russell Brand’s testimony at trial

segments.body: Laura Brand told the jury at Southwark Crown Court that her husband was “caring, kind and a wonderful father”. She said their relationship had ended for a time because he found monogamy difficult, and that they later reunited and married. Her evidence is part of Russell Brand’s defence; it does not determine the allegations.

segments.title: Charges and trial
segments.body: Brand faces three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault relating to six women and allegations spanning 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges. The jury has also heard testimony from Brand and statements from two former partners; it is expected to consider verdicts after the trial concludes.

content.headline: Animal-welfare group reports Danish chicken producer to police
content.shortHeadline: Chicken producer reported over alleged animal-welfare breaches
content.standfirst: The complaint follows TV 2 footage that the broadcaster says shows Ross 308 chickens receiving only three hours of darkness daily, below the six-hour requirement. The producer previously said he had made wrong decisions and tightened procedures.

image.caption: TV 2’s hidden-camera footage shows chickens inside the producer’s farm.

sources.originalTitle: Afslørende billeder af turbokyllinger fører til politianmeldelse

segments.body: Animal-protection organisation Dyrenes Beskyttelse has reported chicken producer Christian Tvergaard to police after TV 2 published undercover footage from his operation. The broadcaster says the footage shows Ross 308 chickens receiving three hours of darkness a day for most of their lives, although regulations require at least six.

segments.title: Questions for the authorities
segments.body: The organisation says the footage also shows birds unable to move or turn and argues that the producer failed to care for sick or injured animals. Tvergaard has declined to comment on the complaint. In a written response after the original report, he said he had made wrong decisions and had tightened procedures, including the light programme.

Denmark’s minister for nature and animal welfare has said he wants to work towards a national ban on fast-growing chickens, subject to legal and economic examination. The complaint is an allegation, not a finding by police or a court.

content.headline: Danish police failed to notify public employer about translator’s conviction
content.shortHeadline: Police admit notification failure in case of convicted hospital
content.standfirst: Fyn Police says it failed to report a public employee’s case through the required channel, allowing her to continue working as a hospital translator after a conviction for document forgery. Police say they have found other cases that should have been reported.

sources.originalTitle: Kriminel tolk ansat på sygehus i årevis – politiet glemte at give besked

segments.body: Fyn Police acknowledges it failed to notify the relevant authorities after a publicly employed Arabic translator was charged in 2023 with taking an identity test for another person. She was later sentenced to three months in prison for document forgery but continued working at Tolkecenter Syddanmark, which provides interpreting for health and social services.

segments.title: Procedures under review
segments.body: The Rigsadvokaten, which informs public employers about employees’ charges and convictions based on police reports, said it had received no notification. Fyn Police called the omission a serious human error and says it is reinforcing procedures; it has also identified other cases that should have been reported. The hospital operator has not confirmed whether the translator remains employed or whether her work will be reviewed.

Employment-law lecturers quoted by TV 2 called the failure serious and said the employer needs reliable information about criminal cases involving staff. One said the conviction could be incompatible with continuing employment as a public-sector translator. The broadcaster says it has sought comment from the woman.

content.headline: Rigshospitalet declined 10 liver offers over staffing capacity
content.shortHeadline: Rigshospitalet turned down liver offers amid staffing limits
content.standfirst: In the past year, Denmark’s national hospital declined three livers for children and seven for adults from the Nordic transplant network because it lacked capacity. The hospital says it has never been staffed for round-the-clock paediatric liver transplants.

image.caption: Rigshospitalet says it has declined liver offers when staffing capacity was insufficient.

source.credit: Foto: Emil Nicolai Helms / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Riget afviser leverdonationer til børn på grund af manglende kapacitet

segments.body: Rigshospitalet declined 10 liver offers from the Nordic transplant collaboration Scandiatransplant in the past 12 months because of staffing capacity: three intended for children and seven for adults, according to information provided by the Capital Region to Sundhedsmonitor. An organ may have to be offered elsewhere if the hospital cannot staff a transplant.

segments.title: Different arrangements elsewhere
segments.body: Rigshospitalet says it has never been staffed to perform paediatric liver transplants 24 hours a day, every day of the year, and says it is not unusual to decline such offers. Oslo University Hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it has a rota that provides staffing and expertise around the clock and has never declined a liver transplant for lack of staff.

The report says a declined offer can mean a Danish patient waits longer and may, in the worst case, die while waiting. A regional politician and the Organ Donation Association are calling for Danish patients to have the same conditions as patients elsewhere in the Nordic network. The Danish Health Authority had not commented by the report’s deadline.

content.headline: Report says Danish ISS subsidiary shared responsibility for Hong Kong fire
content.shortHeadline: Hong Kong fire report criticises Danish ISS subsidiary
content.standfirst: A public inquiry into the fire that killed 168 people says ISS EastPoint had a degree of responsibility, including for allowing an unauthorised worker to disable fire alarms. ISS says other companies bore primary responsibility and that it has strengthened procedures.

image.caption: The fire at Hong Kong’s Wang Fuk Court complex killed 168 people.

sources.originalTitle: 1.200 siders rapport frigivet: Dansk gigant havde medansvar for historisk dødsbrand

segments.body: A Hong Kong inquiry report on the Wang Fuk Court fire, which killed 168 people during renovation work last year, criticises ISS EastPoint Property Management, an ISS subsidiary. The report says an ISS technician disabled the fire-alarm systems in eight residential towers months before the blaze, although the technician was not authorised to work on them.

segments.title: ISS response and ongoing investigation
segments.body: The committee says the disabled alarms meant residents received no fire warning and describes ISS’s approach to fire-safety matters as passive. ISS says the main responsibility rests with the renovation contractor and consultant, and that its subsidiary was not involved in the work or the fire’s origin and spread. It says it has strengthened procedures and staff training.

The report also criticises the handling of smoking and escape-route openings at the site, and criticises authorities’ oversight. Some details were withheld because a criminal investigation is ongoing. Seven people and two companies have been charged; ISS and its employees are not among them.

content.headline: Venstre local politicians criticise leader after MP’s expulsion
content.shortHeadline: Venstre members attack leadership over MP’s expulsion
content.standfirst: Several local politicians in northern Jutland say the party went too far in expelling Preben Bang Henriksen, who would not promise to follow the parliamentary group’s line. Venstre’s regional chair says members must support agreed decisions outside the group room.

image.caption: Venstre leaders address the expulsion of Preben Bang Henriksen.

sources.originalTitle: Nordjysk vrede efter eksklusion af Preben Bang: 'Jeg er led ved at være Venstre-mand lige nu'

segments.body: A number of Venstre local politicians in northern Jutland have criticised party leader Troels Lund Poulsen after MP Preben Bang Henriksen was expelled. Henriksen had refused to promise that he would always vote in line with the parliamentary group. Critics say MPs should be able to disagree on individual issues.

segments.title: Party response and dissent
segments.body: Venstre’s regional chair in North Jutland said the expulsion was Henriksen’s own choice and that members may disagree within the parliamentary group but must support the party’s line outside it. Other local politicians said they understood the leadership’s position, arguing the party needs a unified position. The criticism also includes complaints about Lund Poulsen’s leadership and political direction.

content.headline: Danish court orders Polymarket block lifted while case is reconsidered
content.shortHeadline: Court lifts Denmark’s block on prediction site Polymarket
content.standfirst: The Eastern High Court ruled that Polymarket should have been heard before the original blocking order was made. Internet providers have been asked to lift the block, but the lower court must reconsider whether the site should be blocked again.

image.caption: Polymarket is a prediction-market platform that had been blocked in Denmark.

sources.originalTitle: Nu er omstridt bettingside ikke længere blokeret i Danmark

segments.body: Denmark’s Eastern High Court has ordered the block on Polymarket to be lifted after finding that the prediction-market platform should have been heard as a party in the original case. Danish internet providers say they have asked members to remove the block.

segments.title: Not a final ruling on legality
segments.body: The Gambling Authority brought the case, arguing that the site violated Danish gambling law. A lower court ordered providers to block it in July. The High Court has sent the case back for reconsideration; it has not ruled that Polymarket complies with Danish law or that it can remain available permanently.

content.headline: Nordic dispute over Putin calls exposes divisions on Europe’s role
content.shortHeadline: Nordic leaders clash over direct contact with Putin
content.standfirst: Denmark’s prime minister criticised Finnish and Norwegian leaders for making an uncoordinated call to Vladimir Putin. The callers say Ukraine was consulted and wants Europe involved; analysts say the public dispute risks playing into Moscow’s hands.

image.caption: Mette Frederiksen criticised the lack of coordination over the call to Putin.

sources.originalTitle: Omdiskuteret opkald kaldes "sød musik i Putins ører"
Norsk redaktør: Derfor bad jeg Mette Frederiksen holde kæft
​Pragmatic or pointless? Europe’s rift over whether to pick up the phone to Putin

segments.body: Mette Frederiksen criticised Finland’s president Alexander Stubb and Norway’s prime minister Jonas Gahr Støre for calling Vladimir Putin without coordinating with other European countries. Støre says the call was made at Ukraine’s request, and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has thanked the two leaders. Sweden’s prime minister also said he had not been informed beforehand.

segments.title: Europe’s voice in talks
segments.body: Støre says Europe should have a direct role in discussions with Russia rather than leaving contact to the United States. The Guardian reports that European governments have yet to agree on whether to appoint a representative or who should speak for the bloc. The Nordic dispute reflects a wider argument about when and how Europe should engage Putin.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s reporting adds that Europe has no agreed mandate for a single negotiator, and that the call’s purpose was described in different ways by its participants. Analysts warn that renewed contact should not be mistaken for any sign that Putin is ready to compromise.

segments.title: No reported shift in Russia’s position
segments.body: Danish and other analysts quoted by TV 2 say Russia can use the public disagreement to present Europe as divided. Stubb and Støre say Putin received a clear message, but the reporting gives no indication that he changed his position or offered concessions on Ukraine. What the call achieved remains uncertain.

content.headline: Morphine’s lost demos reveal Mark Sandman’s final years and restless life
content.shortHeadline: Morphine’s lost demos illuminate Mark Sandman’s restless life
content.standfirst: As previously unheard recordings are prepared for release, bandmates and Sandman’s partner recall the music, near-misses and pressures that shaped Morphine—and the grief and care behind a long-delayed posthumous album.

image.caption: Mark Sandman of Morphine.

sources.originalTitle: ​‘He buckled. I could hear his bass ringing out ...’ The luminous rise and tragic end of US alt heroes Morphine

segments.body: Morphine’s 1998 loft demos, recorded before the sessions for the band’s final album with Mark Sandman, are now set for release as Cocoon. The recordings have a looseness that Sandman’s partner, Sabine Hrechdakian, says lets listeners hear him laugh and play; assembling them has felt, she says, like communicating across time.

content.headline: The Big Moon turn Juliette Jackson’s hearing loss into a radiant pop album
content.shortHeadline: The Big Moon turn hearing loss into radiant pop
content.standfirst: After an ear condition left frontperson Juliette Jackson with greatly reduced hearing on one side, she abandoned the songs she found too bleak and wrote toward an imagined happy ending. The review finds that pivot convincing.

image.caption: The Big Moon: Celia Archer, Juliette Jackson, Soph Nathan and Fern Ford.

sources.originalTitle: The Big Moon: Forever review – the hell of hearing loss inspires a defiantly hopeful pop-disco marvel

segments.body: Jackson’s cholesteatoma and the loss of much of her hearing on one side made songwriting feel existentially uncertain. Rather than continue with songs she found miserable, she set out to imagine a happier future. On Forever, the resulting pop-disco brightness carries extra force because it comes from that difficult starting point.

content.headline: Why music fans are returning to CDs—and what streaming cannot offer them
content.shortHeadline: Why music fans are returning to CDs
content.standfirst: Retail searches for CD players and reported sales are rising. Collectors and newer listeners explain the appeal: ownership, a more deliberate way to listen and, for some, a better route to supporting musicians.

image.caption: Young people browsing and listening to CDs in a Munich music shop.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comeback

segments.body: The Guardian reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players at John Lewis since July and cites a separate report that CD sales are up 16%. The people it spoke to describe different paths back to discs, from lifelong collecting to rediscovering CDs as a practical alternative to vinyl.

Several interviewees value choosing and listening to a whole album rather than navigating streaming’s seemingly endless options. Others point to the format’s compactness, the chance to buy directly from smaller acts, or simply the pleasure of owning a physical copy. The story presents streaming as useful for discovery, not necessarily as an either-or choice.

content.headline: How Romford helped shape 90s rave, jungle and UK dance music
content.shortHeadline: How Romford became a 90s dance-music force
content.standfirst: A new exhibition revisits the record shop, pirate radio and club nights that helped turn an outer London suburb into a hub for rave and jungle. The story follows the people and independent networks behind its influence.

image.caption: Boogie Times Records in Romford, a hub of the town’s dance-music scene.

sources.originalTitle: Mega mega mega, going back to Romford! How an outer London suburb became a metropolis for 90s dance music

segments.body: Romford’s dance scene grew around Boogie Times, the record shop opened by Danny Donnelly in 1989, and the independent label Suburban Base. Donnelly used small record runs to compete with better-connected London shops, while local DJs, clubs and pirate radio helped new sounds find an audience.

The scene’s reach extended beyond the town: Suburban Base opened a Los Angeles office and its music found audiences in Brazil. A new exhibition, Mega Mega: Romford’s Suburban Sound Revolution, recreates parts of the scene using original equipment and records its contribution to rave, jungle and later UK dance music.

content.headline: Underscores on the leap from online cult favourite to arena stages
content.shortHeadline: Underscores makes the leap from cult favourite to arenas
content.standfirst: April Grey’s album U has brought new listeners and larger rooms, including a support slot on Charli xcx’s tour. The musician discusses growing up amid San Francisco’s tech boom, writing love songs and learning to push past shyness.

image.caption: Underscores, the recording name of April Grey.

sources.originalTitle: Pop prodigy Underscores: ‘I don’t think Gen Z is a loveless generation’

segments.body: Grey says the songs on U began as an attempt to write nine love songs, a subject she had found difficult to approach. The album followed two more sprawling records, and its focused pop sound has helped take her from an underground following to bigger venues and an arena tour with Charli xcx.

Growing up in San Francisco during the tech boom helped shape Grey’s early world, while discovering Skrillex as a child helped spur her to make music. She says touring at different venue sizes has forced her to rethink how her show works—and that meeting her childhood hero also made her confront how hard it can be to initiate conversations.

content.headline: Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl half-time show
content.shortHeadline: Jay-Z to headline the 2027 Super Bowl show
content.standfirst: The rapper, whose Roc Nation has helped produce the NFL’s half-time entertainment since 2019, will take the stage himself at SoFi Stadium on 14 February 2027. He previously said he was not interested in performing.

image.caption: Jay-Z performing in Paris.

sources.originalTitle: Jay-Z picks headliner for 2027 Super Bowl half-time show … Jay-Z

segments.body: The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Jay-Z as the featured performer for the 2027 Super Bowl half-time show at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. Jay-Z has helped produce the event through Roc Nation’s partnership with the NFL, but his appointment marks a change from his earlier stated reluctance to perform.

The announcement follows the close of Jay-Z’s 30 concert tour at the same stadium. He has not released a solo album since 2017, but the report notes his catalogue of major hits, his 25 Grammy wins and his long career across music, management and entertainment.

content.headline: David Bowie’s lost 1978 Earl’s Court concerts will return as an arena show
content.shortHeadline: Bowie’s lost 1978 concerts return as an arena event
content.standfirst: Director Brett Morgen says footage of two Earl’s Court performances, unseen for nearly 50 years, has been restored for a 2027 arena presentation. The project combines the original concerts with modern screens, lighting and surround sound.

image.caption: David Bowie performing on the Isolar II tour in 1978.

sources.originalTitle: ‘How on earth is this man not sweating?’ The director who spent 10 years painstakingly remastering Bowie’s ‘greatest filmed performance’

segments.body: David Bowie commissioned a film of two 1978 Earl’s Court concerts, but the project was shelved after he was reportedly unhappy with the edit. Director Brett Morgen found the footage in Bowie’s archive while working on Moonage Daydream and describes it as the greatest filmed performance of Bowie’s career.

Morgen and his team spent nearly a decade preparing the footage for a 2027 arena presentation, including more than 1,000 hours of colour grading. The project is designed as a multimedia event, with multiple screens, an integrated lighting package and surround sound rather than a conventional film screening.

content.headline: Olivia Tremor Control’s final album turns loss into a dark psychedelic farewell
content.shortHeadline: Olivia Tremor Control’s final album faces mortality
content.standfirst: The Elephant 6 band’s first album in 27 years was largely recorded before the deaths of Bill Doss and Will Cullen Hart. The review hears familiar psychedelic invention shadowed by grief, time and mortality.

sources.originalTitle: The Same Place

segments.body: The Same Place took shape over many years: most of it was recorded between 2010 and 2012, and other members and collaborators added finishing touches after the deaths of founding members Bill Doss and Will Cullen Hart. The review hears the band’s familiar pop instincts and sound collages, now carrying an especially persistent darkness.

Across songs that circle time, death and return, the album resists a neat narrative arc. Its hazy ambiguity remains part of the group’s appeal, but the circumstances of its making give that uncertainty new poignancy. The review calls it a long-overdue postscript to the Elephant 6 collective’s history.

content.headline: Jafar Panahi receives a new prison sentence in Iran; charges remain unclear
content.shortHeadline: Jafar Panahi receives new prison sentence in Iran
content.standfirst: The award-winning director has been sentenced in absentia to five years and one month, according to his lawyer, who says the charges are unclear. A travel ban, social-media restriction and asset seizure were also ordered.

sources.originalTitle: Iranian film-maker Jafar Panahi given new prison sentence

segments.body: An Iranian court has sentenced Jafar Panahi in absentia to five years and one month in prison and ordered the seizure of his assets, his lawyer Mostafa Nili told the Iranian outlet Emtedad. The court also imposed a two-year travel ban and barred Panahi from social media for two years. The charges behind the latest sentence remain unclear.

Panahi returned to Iran in March after promoting It Was Just an Accident abroad, despite an earlier one-year sentence for “propaganda activities against the system”. His lawyer says Panahi was not notified of the latest hearing date. Artists quoted in the report describe the ruling as an effort to silence independent voices; the director had not been detained when the report was published.

content.headline: Anthony Ippolito on playing Sylvester Stallone in the making of Rocky
content.shortHeadline: Anthony Ippolito on becoming Stallone for I Play Rocky
content.standfirst: In Peter Farrelly’s film about the making of Rocky, Ippolito plays a young Stallone determined to keep the starring role he wrote for himself. The actor describes years of pursuing the part and the transformation it demanded.

image.caption: Anthony Ippolito recreates a scene from Rocky in I Play Rocky.

sources.originalTitle: How did a fishmonger who starred in an adult movie make Rocky? The film about Sylvester Stallone’s amazing triumph

segments.body: Anthony Ippolito began sending audition tapes for the role of Sylvester Stallone before Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky had a script. Farrelly says Ippolito was the first actor considered, and that there was no need to audition anyone else. Ippolito changed his voice, posture and physique to play Stallone, who later contacted him with a positive response.

The film follows Stallone’s struggle to get Rocky made on his terms, including his refusal to give up the title role despite financial pressure. Ippolito describes the story as a love letter to Stallone’s persistence, while the film presents the original production as a scrappy effort made under tight constraints.

content.headline: Boots Riley’s I Love Boosters turns fashion theft into frantic satire
content.shortHeadline: I Love Boosters is Boots Riley’s chaotic fashion caper
content.standfirst: Keke Palmer leads a group of shoplifters who target a billionaire designer in Riley’s fast-moving satire of fashion and exploitation. The review finds a funny, often exhausting film packed with ideas and sensory overload.

image.caption: A scene from I Love Boosters.

sources.originalTitle: I Love Boosters review – supercool outlaw women go shoplifting in Boots Riley’s frantic and funny caper

segments.body: In I Love Boosters, a crew of women steal designer clothes from shops and resell them cheaply, partly in protest against the fashion billionaire played by Demi Moore. Their world grows more complicated when a rival thief challenges them over the conditions in which the clothes are made.

The review describes the film as a cacophonous, fast-cut caper that can be difficult to take but often lands its comedy. Moore’s role, despite the attention around her, is closer to a potent cameo than a conventional starring part.

content.headline: Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård star in folk-horror romance Wicker
content.shortHeadline: Wicker makes an unlikely romance from a wicker husband
content.standfirst: A mocked fisherwoman commissions a basketmaker to make her a husband in this strange blend of folk horror and romance. The review finds Olivia Colman’s performance compelling and the film’s odd mix of sentiment and unease intriguing.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the fisherwoman with Alexander Skarsgård as her wicker husband in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker review – Olivia Colman finds the perfect lover in intriguing folk-horror romance

segments.body: In medieval village life, Olivia Colman’s isolated fisherwoman asks a basketmaker, played by Peter Dinklage, to make her a husband. The wicker figure, played by Alexander Skarsgård, proves attentive and capable, unsettling villagers who had mocked her.

The review places the film in an uneasy space between macabre folk horror and sentimentality. It praises Colman’s grounded performance and finds a peculiar pleasure in the story’s romantic premise, while noting that the film’s comedy can feel underplayed.

content.headline: From The Exorcist to The Thing: horror’s greatest practical effects ranked
content.shortHeadline: Horror’s greatest practical effects, from The Omen to The Thing
content.standfirst: A countdown revisits memorable pre-CGI effects, from The Birds’ attic attack to the transformations in The Thing. It looks at how practical craft made horror’s monsters, mutations and shocks feel physically present.

image.caption: A still from The Exorcist, one of the films in the effects countdown.

sources.originalTitle: Exploding heads, mutant aliens and bursting chests: horror’s greatest special effects – ranked!

segments.body: The list ranges across decades of horror filmmaking, highlighting techniques such as in-camera effects, stop-motion, prosthetics and animatronics. Its examples include the transformations in Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, the head turn in The Exorcist and the creature effects in The Thing.

Rather than treating practical effects as a single style, the selection shows how different artists used them for eeriness, bodily transformation or outright shock. Among its examples are the attic attack in The Birds, the chest-bursting scene in Alien and the increasingly strange forms of the Antarctic creature in The Thing.

content.headline: Gentle Monster examines two women’s loyalty to troubled men
content.shortHeadline: Gentle Monster tests loyalty to the men women love
content.standfirst: Léa Seydoux plays a musician whose husband comes under police investigation, while Jella Haase is a detective confronting wrongdoing closer to home. The review calls Marie Kreutzer’s drama cold, unsettling and powered by two strong leads.

image.caption: Léa Seydoux in Gentle Monster, directed by Marie Kreutzer.

sources.originalTitle: Gentle Monster review – disquieting drama about two women facing the truth about the men they love

segments.body: When police search the home of Lucy Weiss, a French musician living in Munich with her husband and son, her husband offers explanations that she struggles to accept. Detective Elsa, investigating the case, is pursuing a suspect at work while making excuses for her father’s misconduct at home.

The film’s central tension is uncertainty about what Lucy’s husband has done and whether their child is involved. The review praises the contrasting performances of Seydoux and Haase and describes the film as bleak, disquieting and focused on the compromises of loyalty and care.

content.headline: Twelve scary films to watch with children this Halloween
content.shortHeadline: 12 scary films for a family Halloween night
content.standfirst: This family-focused Halloween guide ranges from animated ghost stories to classic haunted-house films. It includes age ratings and advises care with younger viewers, so families can choose a level of fright that suits them.

image.caption: An illustrated guide to scary films for family Halloween viewing.

sources.originalTitle: 12 scary films you can actually watch with your kids this Halloween

segments.body: The recommendations span Coraline, Goosebumps, Gremlins, The Others and Poltergeist, among other titles. The selection balances supernatural scares and comic monsters with films the writer considers suitable for older children or teens, while cautioning that parental judgement still matters.

content.headline: Peter Medak, director of The Krays and The Changeling, dies aged 88
content.shortHeadline: Peter Medak, director of The Krays, dies aged 88
content.standfirst: The British-Hungarian filmmaker’s varied career ranged from acclaimed stage adaptations and cult horror to crime films and high-profile television. His family said he died peacefully in Los Angeles.

image.caption: Peter Medak directing A Day in the Death of Joe Egg in 1972.

sources.originalTitle: Peter Medak, veteran director of The Krays and The Changeling, dies aged 88

segments.body: Peter Medak, who directed The Changeling, The Krays and Let Him Have It, has died aged 88, his family announced. His career also included A Day in the Death of Joe Egg and The Ruling Class, alongside episodes of television dramas including Homicide: Life on the Street, The Wire and Breaking Bad.

Born in Hungary in 1937, Medak escaped to Britain after the Hungarian uprising and entered the film industry through newsreel production. After the costly failure of Ghost in the Noonday Sun, he rebuilt his reputation with The Changeling, a film Martin Scorsese later named among his favourite horror movies.

content.headline: Nocturne puts Stephen Graham at the centre of a chilling serial-killer thriller
content.shortHeadline: Stephen Graham chills as a serial killer in Nocturne
content.standfirst: Graham plays a manipulative murderer whose influence reaches beyond his prison cell, drawing a young nurse and an undercover FBI agent into danger. The review is gripped by his performance but finds the wider series uneven.

image.caption: Stephen Graham as Jurek Walter in Nocturne.

sources.originalTitle: Nocturne review – Stephen Graham is TV’s most evil serial killer … and it’s impossible to stop watching him

segments.body: Stephen Graham plays Jurek Walter, a convicted serial killer serving life in a psychiatric hospital. When a missing child reappears after years away, investigator Jonah Lynn returns to the case, and FBI agent Saga goes undercover at the facility to find out what Walter may know.

The review finds Graham’s stillness, unsettling laughter and quiet manipulation compelling, and describes Nocturne as a slow-burning thriller. It also argues that some characters are underdeveloped and that the series gives too little attention to the wider suffering caused by Walter’s crimes.

content.headline: Murder in Belfast follows the McCartney sisters’ fight for justice
content.shortHeadline: The McCartney sisters’ long fight for justice
content.standfirst: After Robert McCartney was killed in Belfast in 2005, his five sisters challenged intimidation and pressed for answers. This three-part documentary follows their campaign and its impact on the Northern Ireland peace process.

image.caption: Paula McCartney in Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice.

sources.originalTitle: Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice review – a family’s astonishing bravery helped make history

segments.body: Robert McCartney was killed after a fight at a Belfast bar involving members of the Provisional IRA. The documentary follows his sisters as they seek justice amid a lack of witnesses and what the family describes as a wall of silence. The sisters took their campaign to the United States, meeting President George W Bush and senators.

A court case against three men began in 2008 but collapsed amid weak physical evidence and flawed witness testimony. The review sees the sisters’ persistence as historically consequential, while stressing that the family’s long campaign remains marked by grief and loss.

content.headline: Escaping Idi Amin recounts Ugandan Asians’ flight and new lives in Britain
content.shortHeadline: Ugandan Asians recall fleeing Idi Amin’s purge
content.standfirst: Four people who were children when Idi Amin ordered Asian Ugandans to leave describe the violence and fear they witnessed. The review connects their experiences to Britain’s response and the homes they later built there.

image.caption: A reconstruction of Harminder and his father’s escape from Uganda to Britain.

sources.originalTitle: Escaping Idi Amin review – there’s a happy ending to this awful tale … and it should be a lesson to us all

segments.body: The two-part documentary follows four people who were born in Uganda and later became British citizens. They recall the shift from ordinary childhood life to threats and violence after Amin ordered about 80,000 Asian Ugandans to leave the country within 90 days in 1972.

The review also examines the hostility some refugees faced in Britain and the family members lost or left behind. The contributors built new lives in the UK, but the critic argues that the memories of what they witnessed remain painful and carry an urgent lesson about scapegoating and sanctuary.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors’ Miranda Hart brings warmth to a ruthless game
content.shortHeadline: Miranda Hart brings warmth to The Celebrity Traitors
content.standfirst: The comedian’s exit from the celebrity competition has prompted a renewed appreciation of her humour and openness. The piece links that response to her return to television after a period of illness.

image.caption: Miranda Hart in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Miranda has brought wholesome joy back to TV

segments.body: After seven episodes of The Celebrity Traitors, Miranda Hart was murdered by the Traitors. The article recalls her series highlights, from comic mishaps to a dance lesson with Leigh-Anne, and argues that her warmth and willingness to be vulnerable made her a favourite of viewers and fellow contestants.

Hart has spoken about chronic fatigue syndrome and years when she was largely bed-bound. She described appearing on the show as a chance to return to professional work and to the human connection and laughter she feared might no longer be possible.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future follows a long history of reinvention
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after its latest reset
content.standfirst: With the BBC’s Disney+ partnership ended, no new Doctor announced and a planned Christmas special cancelled, the show’s future is unclear. Fans and television voices weigh what has changed—and what could bring it back.

image.caption: Several of Doctor Who’s recent Doctors, including Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: After Ncuti Gatwa’s Doctor left the series, the BBC ended its collaboration with Disney+ and cancelled a planned Christmas special. The programme is being offered for competitive tender, but the article says no new production partner had stepped forward when it was published.

Fans and television writers quoted in the article disagree about what went wrong, pointing to scripts, the production partnership and the show’s long-running changes of Doctor and showrunner. Some see the current silence as a break; others fear a much-loved institution is being left off air for too long.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a new British Asian family into the legal drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to the fore
content.standfirst: Abi Morgan’s spin-off moves the family-law drama to Manchester, with Ritu Arya and Sanjeev Bhaskar among its cast. Its creators say the series pairs familiar relationship drama with broader representation behind and in front of the camera.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows a Manchester family-run law firm handling high-stakes divorce cases. Ritu Arya plays Aria, a barrister expected to take over from her father, played by Sanjeev Bhaskar, until a family death and a former romantic connection complicate her plans.

Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to portray British Asian characters living ordinary lives rather than confining them to familiar stereotypes. Original series creator Abi Morgan describes her role as supporting a new writing team, and says the spin-off keeps family and relationship drama at its core.

content.headline: Seven new and returning series to watch in November
content.shortHeadline: Seven TV picks to watch in November
content.standfirst: The November guide ranges from a Muhammad Ali drama and a new Blade Runner series to returning spy thriller Black Doves and comedy from Amy Poehler. Release dates and platforms vary by territory.

sources.originalTitle: The Greatest to Blade Runner 2099: 12 of the best TV shows to watch this November

segments.body: Among the featured dramas is The Greatest, which follows Muhammad Ali from childhood through the early years of his boxing career. The guide also picks the second season of Black Doves and a new adaptation of Karin Slaughter’s The Good Daughter, with release dates and services listed for the US and UK.

The selection also includes Dig, a comedy from Amy Poehler and Mike Schur about archaeologists who uncover a priceless artefact, and Blade Runner 2099, starring Michelle Yeoh. The entry for the latter describes a future in which replicants hunt humans, reversing the premise familiar from the films.

content.headline: Night Plane turns a flight-attendant job sim into existential horror
content.shortHeadline: Night Plane’s flight-attendant shift descends into horror
content.standfirst: This low-poly indie game begins with routine airport work before a crash sends its attendant into an unsettling loop of demons, flickering lights and strange passengers. The review praises its humour and disturbing imagination.

image.caption: A scene from Night Plane.

sources.originalTitle: Night Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head trip

segments.body: Night Plane starts with check-ins and in-flight service, then turns a routine job simulator into a nightmare. After a crash, the player is back at the airport, sorting ordinary passengers from demons and trying to understand what happened.

The review praises the game’s glitchy, low-poly visuals, which evoke the limitations of early PlayStation games, and its shifts between deadpan comedy and genuine unease. It takes about four or five hours to complete, with later playthroughs offering additional quests and endings.

content.headline: AI tools are making elaborate video-game mashups easier to build
content.shortHeadline: AI makes video-game mashups easier—and raises new risks
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s games columnist reports that AI-assisted decompiling can help people modify games in hours rather than months. The change lowers the technical barrier but sharpens questions about piracy, copyright and ownership.

image.caption: A video-game mashup combining elements of Minecraft and Fortnite.

sources.originalTitle: Social media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from?

segments.body: The article traces viral clips of unusual game mashups to AI-assisted coding. It describes how tools such as Claude can help reverse compiled game code into a form people can edit, making some ambitious modifications possible in far less time than before, though human work remains involved.

The author says the same access raises serious concerns for game publishers, as emulation and modified versions can make copyrighted games easier to circulate without permission. The piece leaves open whether the spread of AI-assisted tools will prompt AI companies to limit their capabilities.

content.headline: Eight indie horror games for Halloween, from folk tales to haunted takeaways
content.shortHeadline: Eight indie horror games for Halloween
content.standfirst: This seasonal guide ranges from a dark fairy-tale adventure to a Scottish takeaway horror and a devilish card game. It offers a mix of styles for players looking for something eerie this Halloween.

image.caption: The Killing Stone, a horror game featured in the Halloween guide.

sources.originalTitle: Eight great new indie horror games for Halloween

segments.body: The recommendations include Allogloom, a picture-book-style adventure about a girl searching for her mother; The Killing Stone, a card game against the devil; and a short horror set in a Scottish takeaway, with dialogue in Scottish Gaelic (Gàidhlig).

Other picks include a game about a penguin observing cosmic horrors at an Antarctic Nazi base, a haunted-town mystery and an adventure that combines pixel art with live-action sequences. The guide favours varied indie approaches over a single kind of scare.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans grieving a lost RPG future
content.shortHeadline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans bereft
content.standfirst: EA has closed the studio behind Mass Effect and cancelled its forthcoming game, according to this first-person account. A longtime fan reflects on the series’ lasting appeal: consequential choices, memorable companions and a galaxy shaped by players.

image.caption: Mass Effect 3, part of BioWare’s acclaimed science-fiction role-playing series.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: The article reports that EA closed BioWare, ending development of its next Mass Effect game and costing more than 400 people their jobs. Its author, a longtime fan and games-industry worker, mourns the studio’s loss while acknowledging its recent lack of a major critical or commercial hit.

The writer recalls how the original trilogy made decisions carry across games and gave its companions complex personal stories. That sense of agency, the article argues, helped establish the series’ reputation—and makes the cancellation of another instalment feel like a lost possibility, not just a studio closure.

content.headline: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 delivers a bombastic campaign and packed modes
content.shortHeadline: Modern Warfare 4 is a polished, high-speed thrill ride
content.standfirst: The review finds a short but polished campaign, lively multiplayer and a detailed extraction mode, while questioning how well the package can hold players against established rivals. It also notes the series’ gung-ho view of conflict.

image.caption: A scene from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

sources.originalTitle: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game

segments.body: Modern Warfare 4’s six-hour campaign moves from rooftop parkour in Manhattan to a battle at a North Korean airbase. The review calls it a fast, polished action ride, though it says the Captain Price storyline loses some emotional weight towards the end.

Multiplayer builds on the speed of Black Ops 7, with new modes and shifting maps. The returning extraction mode DMZ adds a safehouse, upgrades and missions, but the reviewer has only played an early-access version and says its success will depend on attracting and retaining players.

content.headline: A father and son revisit the Call of Duty missions they never finished
content.shortHeadline: A father and son finish a Call of Duty mission, 17 years on
content.standfirst: A father and his 22-year-old son return to the co-op missions they began when the son was five. Their different play styles give way to teamwork, turning an old game into a moving record of shared time.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game the writer and his son play together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his son replay the Modern Warfare 2 co-op missions they first attempted when the boy was five. This time, the father advances cautiously while his son rushes ahead; they fail repeatedly before finding a compromise and completing a mission they had left unfinished for 17 years.

More than a review of a game, the essay is about the pleasure of playing together and the memories that accumulate around it. The pair expect to move to different parts of the world in a few months, making their late-night sessions feel all the more precious.

content.headline: Does courting a game character count as cheating? GTA VI debate explained
content.shortHeadline: Is romancing a game character really cheating?
content.standfirst: Online arguments about Grand Theft Auto VI’s fictional couple have raised real questions about boundaries and loneliness. The article weighs the claims without treating every relationship as having the same rules.

image.caption: GTA VI protagonists Lucia and Jason.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: Players will be able to strengthen the bond between GTA VI protagonists Lucia and Jason through dates, messages and other interactions. Some social-media users say that taking part in such a fictional romance amounts to cheating, a debate the article traces through TikTok and other platforms.

The writer rejects a blanket rule that in-game romance is unfaithful, while acknowledging that partners can set different boundaries. The article argues that some objections may reflect genuine concerns about feeling neglected, and distinguishes playing a game from AI services designed to simulate intimate relationships.

content.headline: Tiny medical robots could deliver drugs more precisely—but most are experimental
content.shortHeadline: Tiny medical robots aim for more precise drug delivery
content.standfirst: Swallowable capsules already carry cameras through the gut, while researchers are testing much smaller, magnetically guided devices. Some have delivered drugs in animals, but bloodstream treatments remain experimental.

image.caption: Illustration of a miniature medical robot designed to deliver drugs in the gut.

sources.originalTitle: The astonishing micro-robots you swallow that spot cancer and might help treat it

segments.body: Medical robots range from camera capsules used to examine the gut to experimental devices designed to deliver drugs at a precise location. Researchers in Beijing reported using a 6.5mm magnetic “spiny milli-ball” to deliver insulin to the lower intestine of pigs. It has not been shown to work as a treatment in people.

segments.title: From the gut to the bloodstream
segments.body: Other researchers have guided a 2mm robot through a pig’s bloodstream and used a device in a model of the brain’s circulation to deliver a clot-dissolving drug. These demonstrations point to possible future uses, including treating tumours or localised infections, but do not establish that such treatments are safe or effective in patients.

The proposed advantage is precision: releasing a drug at its target might reduce the amount needed elsewhere in the body. Researchers are also exploring swarms of still smaller magnetic particles; one group has shown tumour heating in mice. The field is promising, but much of the work remains at an early stage.

content.headline: Optogenetics partially restored vision in six patients in an early trial
content.shortHeadline: Light-based gene therapy helped some patients regain sight
content.standfirst: In a study of 10 people with retinitis pigmentosa, six gained enough vision in one treated eye to perform tasks such as picking up a cup. The approach does not restore normal sight, and other uses remain in development.

image.caption: Light can provide precise control over nerve cells.

sources.originalTitle: A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: A gene therapy using optogenetics—making nerve cells respond to light—partially improved vision in six of 10 people with retinitis pigmentosa, according to a study published in The New England Journal of Medicine. Participants received treatment in one eye and wore special glasses that convert light into amber wavelengths.

segments.title: A limited but measurable change
segments.body: Before treatment, participants were blind in the treated eye or could, at most, detect a hand waving in front of them. After three months, six could complete tasks such as picking up a cup. They did not regain normal vision or the ability to distinguish faces, and had to train to interpret the new visual signals.

segments.title: Other possible uses are further away
segments.body: Researchers are also exploring optogenetic approaches to pain, epilepsy and hearing loss. These are at earlier stages: the hearing work described is being tested in animals, and applying gene therapy to the ear may carry risks. The approach’s potential in other conditions should not be mistaken for an established treatment.

content.headline: Cancer-detecting electronic nose remains in development as researchers build its
content.shortHeadline: Researchers are building an electronic nose for cancer detection
content.standfirst: A charity is using donated funds to expand testing of a prototype modelled on dogs’ scent-detection abilities. Researchers are comparing its results with trained dogs; it is not yet a validated NHS screening test.

image.caption: Florin the Labrador was trained to identify prostate cancer by smelling urine samples.

sources.originalTitle: Jo Malone donates £100k for cancer-detecting 'nose'

segments.body: Medical Detection Dogs and quantum physicist Andreas Mershin are developing an electronic device intended to detect prostate cancer from urine. It uses protein-based odour receptors and AI to identify patterns in their activation. The charity says its prototype is being tested on 500 patient samples from Milton Keynes Hospital.

segments.title: Testing the idea
segments.body: Dogs trained by the charity previously identified which samples were cancerous. Researchers plan to compare those results with the electronic nose’s performance. A £100,000 donation from Jo Malone will help the charity install equipment to let dogs process more samples and generate further data for the project.

The work is intended to establish whether scent patterns could eventually support an electronic diagnostic device. The charity and its research partner have described a possible future role in prostate cancer screening and early diagnosis, but the supplied reporting does not establish the prototype’s accuracy or readiness for clinical use.

content.headline: UK report warns rising ADHD diagnoses could bring overdiagnosis—but stops short
content.shortHeadline: Rising ADHD diagnoses prompt warning, not proof of overdiagnosis
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned review says diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism among some young people are approaching or exceeding estimates of how common the conditions are. It stresses that the evidence does not show overdiagnosis is already widespread.

image.caption: A young person looks at a phone as diagnoses of ADHD and autism rise.

sources.originalTitle: The four reasons why ADHD experts fear the UK is heading towards overdiagnosis

segments.body: A UK government-commissioned report warns that rapidly rising diagnoses of ADHD and autism may increase the risk of overdiagnosis. Among teenage boys, the proportion diagnosed with ADHD rose from 2% to 5% over a decade; among girls of the same age, it rose from 0.5% to 2.5%. The review says rates for some groups are approaching or exceeding estimates of prevalence.

segments.title: The report is a warning, not a verdict
segments.body: The authors say the available research does not, by itself, establish that overdiagnosis is currently occurring at scale. They point to factors that complicate diagnosis, including conditions assessed through behaviour rather than a blood test or scan, changing definitions, greater awareness and the role of private clinics.

The review also cautions that underdiagnosis and misdiagnosis remain concerns. Some people may be missing support, while symptoms such as anxiety can resemble ADHD. The report calls for better oversight of private assessment services as the NHS faces long waits for diagnosis.

content.headline: UK flu season has started early, but that does not mean it will be severe
content.shortHeadline: Early flu rise is no guarantee of a worse season
content.standfirst: Flu infections are rising in the UK earlier than usual, with experts discussing several possible explanations. Health officials say the early start alone cannot predict how severe the season will be and urge eligible people to get vaccinated.

image.caption: Winter viruses are rising in the UK earlier than usual this year.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are sick right now

segments.body: UK flu activity is rising earlier than usual, according to the UK Health Security Agency, though levels were still relatively low in October. Researchers and health officials are considering whether changes in circulating strains or infections carried from the southern hemisphere could help explain the timing.

segments.title: Timing does not predict severity
segments.body: Experts say an early start does not necessarily mean more people will die or become seriously ill. Flu seasons vary, and the previous season also began early before ending with fewer flu deaths than average. Scientists are still debating why respiratory viruses tend to peak in winter and why the timing changes from year to year.

Flu tends to come on quickly and can bring fever, chills and muscle aches; colds more often cause a runny nose, sneezing and a sore throat, although symptoms can overlap. The UKHSA is urging people eligible for an NHS flu vaccine to take it up rather than assume it will protect against other winter viruses.

content.headline: An essay questions the ‘best baby’ promise of embryo trait selection
content.shortHeadline: The ‘best baby’ pitch raises questions beyond the science
content.standfirst: A writer with a disability examines commercial embryo screening and argues that claims about selecting traits can turn population-level genetic estimates into misleading promises about individuals. The essay also asks whose idea of “best” is being sold.

image.caption: Illustration accompanying an essay on embryo selection and the idea of a “best baby”.

sources.originalTitle: Would you pay to have the ‘best baby’? Liberal eugenics and the troubling quest for human perfection

segments.body: In a personal essay, Ryan Evans reflects on the return of commercial claims about choosing a “best baby” through embryo screening. He argues that estimates of how much genes contribute to traits such as height or intelligence describe variation across populations; they do not mean parents can reliably choose how tall or intelligent an individual child will be.

segments.title: The ethical questions
segments.body: Evans places expanded genetic selection in the history of eugenics, while distinguishing present-day consumer choice from earlier state coercion. His argument is that a market promise of optimisation can still imply that some traits—and the people who have them—are less desirable. The essay is explicitly an argument about the social meaning and limits of selection, not a report that the technology can deliver a perfect child.

Drawing on his own experience of disability, Evans argues for improving the conditions in which people live rather than treating the elimination of disability as the only route to a worthwhile life.
