He does not reject cures or treatments; he challenges the idea that medical selection can define a single ideal human future.

content.headline: Ofcom proposes four ways to check ages ahead of the UK social media ban
content.shortHeadline: Ofcom outlines age checks for the UK’s under-16 social media ban
content.standfirst: Photo ID matching, bank-based checks, digital ID and facial age estimation are among the options Ofcom says could help establish whether users are 16 or older. The government is due to consider the guidance before deciding how the ban will work.

sources.originalTitle: Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s

segments.body: Ofcom has recommended four ways social media companies could check whether users are old enough under the UK’s planned ban on under-16s: matching a live image to photo ID, checks using information held by banks, facial age estimation and digital ID services. The government is expected to consider the guidance before making a decision by the end of the year.

segments.title: Responsibility and limitations
segments.body: Ofcom says companies should choose methods that preserve privacy and protect personal data, rather than follow a single prescribed system. The regulator says providers remain responsible for carrying out checks, even if phone operating systems add age controls. It also acknowledges that some children may bypass the measures.

The proposals could require many adults to prove they meet the age limit, too. Child-safety groups welcomed the guidance while stressing that firms must be held accountable; the Molly Rose Foundation also questioned Ofcom’s record of enforcing online-safety rules.

content.headline: A hack exposed records on 41,000 US homeland security staff; access to the
content.shortHeadline: Hack exposes thousands of US homeland security staff records
content.standfirst: A group of hackers says it accessed more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security personnel records, including names and work contact details. The department says it is investigating a potential breach; the route of access remains disputed.

sources.originalTitle: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
Bluesky blocks links to leaked DHS employee data as government seeks takedowns

segments.body: More than 41,000 records concerning Department of Homeland Security personnel, including staff at Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, were published online. The dataset reportedly contains names, work addresses, phone numbers and descriptions of roles. The department says it is aware of a potential breach and is working to address it.

segments.title: How the data was obtained is not settled
segments.body: The group behind the leak says it accessed employee profiles through the Okta single sign-on service. Okta says it has no evidence its systems or data were compromised. The published records also include operation names and information about technology used by some agencies, according to the reporting.

segments.title: A dispute over public access
segments.body: Bluesky blocked links to DDoSecrets, which hosts the leaked dataset, marking them as malicious. DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best argues the material contains professional rather than home contact information and says it could assist public-records requests. The Department of Homeland Security sought removal of a searchable site, saying the data includes personal contact and location information.

perspectives.body: DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best says the dataset contains professional contact details, not home addresses, and argues that the information is relevant to public-records requests.

content.headline: Apple says it will replace some iPhone Duo units after screen faults
content.shortHeadline: Apple offers replacements for some iPhone Duo screen faults
content.standfirst: Some buyers of Apple’s first foldable phone have reported lines, cracks or noises around the inner display. Apple says a small number of devices are affected and is asking users with problems to contact the company; the scale is not yet clear.

image.caption: An iPhone Duo user said Apple helped replace a handset with screen faults.

sources.originalTitle: Apple to replace iPhone Duos affected by screen problem

segments.body: Apple says it is aware of an issue affecting the inner displays of a small number of its new foldable iPhone Duo handsets and has asked affected users to contact the company for a replacement. Users have posted images of screen lines and cracks near the centre hinge, as well as reports of a crunching sound when opening the device.

segments.title: The extent remains unclear
segments.body: Apple has not said how many phones are affected. Some images circulating online may have been generated with AI, an IDC analyst cautioned, so reports do not establish a widespread manufacturing fault. The hinge and folding screen are complex components, and rivals have faced similar early issues with foldable devices.

content.headline: DoorDash agrees to buy Instacart in a $17bn delivery-platform deal
content.shortHeadline: DoorDash to acquire Instacart for $17bn
content.standfirst: The proposed acquisition would bring restaurant delivery leader DoorDash and grocery delivery company Instacart under one owner. Both boards have approved the deal, but the companies say they will continue to operate separately until it closes.

sources.originalTitle: DoorDash to acquire Instacart for $17B

segments.body: DoorDash has agreed to acquire Instacart for $17bn, valuing the deal at $65 for each Instacart share. The boards of both companies approved the transaction. DoorDash says it plans to keep the Instacart brand, app and enterprise technology products, with the two businesses operating independently until the deal closes.

segments.title: A combined delivery and retail toolkit
segments.body: DoorDash says the deal could let more grocery retailers use Instacart’s online ordering and advertising technology alongside DoorDash’s fulfilment network. The companies describe the combination as a way to offer retailers more delivery options, but the supplied reporting does not establish what changes customers will see if the acquisition goes ahead.

The transaction is expected to close in late 2027 or the first half of 2028. Instacart’s shares had risen 25% year to date, and Bloomberg had previously reported that it held talks with Uber before those discussions ended.

content.headline: An open-source project helps some Withings scale owners sync data without
content.shortHeadline: An open-source workaround restores third-party syncing for some With
content.standfirst: YourOwnWeigh reroutes data from two older Withings smart-scale models to other services without a Withings Plus subscription. The workaround needs alternate firmware and a server, and its creator hopes to extend support to more apps and devices.

sources.originalTitle: This open-source project lets you sync Withings data to other apps without a subscription

segments.body: An open-source project called YourOwnWeigh offers owners of two older Withings smart scales a way to send their weigh-in data to other apps without paying for Withings Plus. Its creator, Tom Anthony, built it after Withings said new users would need a subscription to sync data with third-party services.

segments.title: A workaround with limits
segments.body: The web app patches the scales’ firmware so they send data to a server chosen by the user, who can run it on their own or use a free Cloudflare account. Anthony used Apple Shortcuts to transfer the data into Apple Health. The project currently supports only two older models, and wider app compatibility remains a goal rather than an existing feature.

content.headline: Anthropic’s IPO filing lays out huge ambitions, risks and spending obligations
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic’s IPO filing puts AI’s risks and economics in focus
content.standfirst: The AI company reported $16.3bn in first-half revenue and losses above $80bn, much of the loss tied to accounting charges. Its filing also warns of potential catastrophic risks from advanced AI and lays out substantial infrastructure commitments.

image.caption: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying
Anthropic is asking Wall Street to believe in AGI

segments.body: Anthropic’s filing ahead of a planned US stock-market listing reports $16.3bn in revenue for the first half of 2026 and losses of more than $80bn. The company says it needs extensive access to chips and data centres to develop its models. The loss figure includes large accounting charges; it should not be read on its own as a measure of cash spent.

segments.title: A business tied to growth
segments.body: The filing describes large commitments for computing capacity and infrastructure. The Verge’s analysis estimates at least $850bn in commitments over up to 20 years, while stressing that the company does not provide a simple total payment schedule. Its columnist argues the business depends on rapid growth and continued model improvements to meet those obligations.

perspectives.body: The Verge’s analysis sees Anthropic’s long-term commitments as making growth essential, and questions whether rapid model-driven expansion can deliver the returns the business appears to require.

segments.title: The investment case remains contested
segments.body: Analyst Joey Brookhart, interviewed by The Verge, presents a more optimistic view: he points to rising efficiency and strong margins on inference as potential support for continued investment. Anthropic, meanwhile, warns investors that sufficiently advanced systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks if developed or deployed without safeguards. Both the company’s projections and the eventual safety implications remain uncertain.

perspectives.body: Analyst Joey Brookhart argues that improving compute efficiency and demand across new business areas could support Anthropic’s growth, while acknowledging that the company’s ambitions depend on uncertain future adoption.

content.headline: Companies are giving AI agents office jobs, but workers still have to check
content.shortHeadline: AI agents take on office tasks, while humans manage the mistakes
content.standfirst: Some startups now rely on far more software agents than human staff to handle tasks from coding to recruitment. Workers describe time savings and new capabilities, alongside errors, job concerns and the loss of human contact.

image.caption: AI agents have become a status symbol among some San Francisco startups.

sources.originalTitle: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?

segments.body: Startups are assigning AI agents work once done by executive assistants, recruiters, marketers and other employees. At one company profiled by the Guardian, 15 people work alongside roughly 150 agents. Large organisations’ reported use of agents has also grown, although research cited in the report has not yet found major productivity gains from AI overall.

segments.title: More delegation—and more checking
segments.body: Workers say agents can run tasks in parallel, prepare schedules and draft marketing materials. But they still need people to set them up and review the output: one startup executive said an agent confused candidates with similar names and invented résumé details. Employees also worry that automating entry-level work could make it harder for new workers to get experience.

segments.title: The human interaction cost
segments.body: Some companies use agents to contact customers or job candidates, but several people interviewed said automated outreach can feel impersonal or waste their time. One company’s founder has barred agents from customer communications. The reporting suggests that adoption may change not only who does office work, but also what customers and colleagues expect from one another.

content.headline: Arizona’s data-centre boom meets a growing fight over water and local
content.shortHeadline: Arizona residents challenge data-centre plans over water and power
content.standfirst: In drought-strained Arizona, residents are pushing back against large data-centre proposals, citing water, electricity and land use. The debate also highlights how the state’s semiconductor boom differs from projects that opponents say offer fewer lasting jobs.

image.caption: An irrigation canal carrying Colorado River water to Phoenix.

sources.originalTitle: AI has come for Arizona’s water

segments.body: Large data-centre proposals in Arizona have provoked opposition from residents concerned about water, power and the effects on local communities. In Tucson, a proposed 600-megawatt complex drew protests and new local restrictions. Though city officials rejected annexation of the site, the developer later continued with the project, according to the reporting.

segments.title: Different projects, different trade-offs
segments.body: The story contrasts proposed data centres with TSMC’s semiconductor operations in Phoenix, which use millions of gallons of water daily but have also brought thousands of jobs and a supplier network. TSMC says it recycles much of its water and is working toward higher reuse. Critics raise separate concerns about industrial chemicals and wastewater, which the company says it monitors and treats.

segments.title: Competing claims about the costs
segments.body: Beale Infrastructure says its Tucson project switched to air cooling and that its water use once operating will be limited to ordinary needs such as kitchens and restrooms. Local opponents dispute the project’s broader resource impact, including the water needed to generate electricity. Arizona’s water pressures predate the AI boom and also reflect agriculture, declining river supplies and groundwater use.

perspectives.body: Beale says the Tucson project’s air-cooling design will not increase overall energy use and that operational water use will be limited to ordinary domestic purposes; local opponents challenge the project’s overall resource costs.

content.headline: UK plans stricter tests for data centres as Northumberland considers more
content.shortHeadline: Proposed data-centre tests win a cautious welcome in Northumberland
content.standfirst: The government says new data centres should deliver local jobs and community benefits while protecting water supplies. In Northumberland, where one large project has been approved and two more are being considered, local leaders disagree on whether the plans go far enough.

image.caption: Two data-centre applications are being considered in Northumberland, where one has already been approved.

sources.originalTitle: New data centres must bring 'local benefits'

segments.body: The UK government says new data centres will face “strict tests” and should invest in local communities, create jobs and protect water supplies. In Northumberland, where QTS has approval for a £10bn facility at Cambois and two further applications are being considered, the announcement received a cautious welcome.

segments.title: Jobs and safeguards under debate
segments.body: Northumberland County Council leader Glen Sanderson called data-centre development important to the economy if handled carefully. Local MP Ian Lavery welcomed the pledge but said its details matter, questioning whether the rules would address the impact of several facilities concentrated in a small area and the use of scarce industrial land.

content.headline: AI psychics promise readings, but experts raise concerns about trust and
content.shortHeadline: AI psychics raise questions about privacy, trust and human guidance
content.standfirst: Apps and social media accounts offer AI-generated readings, sometimes for a fee. Practitioners and researchers question the systems’ claims, the loss of human context and how sensitive conversations are handled.

image.caption: Illustration of an AI-generated psychic on a mobile app.

sources.originalTitle: Computerized clairvoyance: psychics push back against AI-generated readings

segments.body: AI-generated psychics are appearing in apps, on TikTok Live and on online marketplaces. One app sells readings through paid question packages, while some human practitioners now add “no AI” conditions to their services. The market is difficult to assess because the models behind many of these products are not transparent.

segments.title: Guidance without human context
segments.body: Practitioners interviewed by the Guardian say a chatbot cannot provide the empathy and personal connection they consider central to their work. Anthropologist Sally Applin argues that people may treat a chatbot as an oracle, but that it generates answers from statistical patterns and lacks the personal and cultural context of human relationships.

segments.title: Sensitive conversations, unclear handling
segments.body: Some users may share information about relationships, health, finances or mental state. MystiCall says it does not sell private conversations or use them to train its own models; its co-founder describes the service as a way to explore emotions rather than predict the future or diagnose mental illness. The reporting also found that another app’s privacy policy did not address sensitive information.

perspectives.body: MystiCall co-founder Laurie-Anne Bernard says the app does not claim supernatural powers or reliable predictions, and frames its readings as a way to explore emotions and perspectives.

content.headline: Australia move ahead in Cape Town as Labuschagne hits a record low
content.shortHeadline: Australia move ahead as Labuschagne hits a record low
content.standfirst: Australia reached 330-4 on day two of the decisive Test, leading South Africa by one run. Marnus Labuschagne made a duck, extending his wait for a century to a record 48 consecutive innings.

image.caption: Marnus Labuschagne has not scored a Test century since 2023.

sources.originalTitle: Labuschagne's form hits record low but Australia hint at future

segments.body: Labuschagne lasted five balls before edging Simon Harmer to slip. He has now gone 48 consecutive innings without a Test century, a record for a batter in Australia's top four. His last came at Old Trafford in 2023; since then, he has averaged 24.77.

segments.title: Australia's younger batters respond
segments.body: After South Africa were bowled out for 329, Australia were 58-2 when Labuschagne fell. Matt Renshaw made 74, Cameron Green 65 and Josh Inglis was 85 not out, sharing an unbroken stand of 145 with Alex Carey. Australia lead by one run with six wickets in hand, but the Test is not decided.

content.headline: Stan Wawrinka retires after an emotional final match in Basel
content.shortHeadline: Wawrinka bows out after emotional Basel defeat
content.standfirst: The three-time Grand Slam champion's 23-year professional career ended with a two-set loss to Jiri Lehecka in front of his home crowd. Wawrinka leaves the sport after a career that defied expectations.

image.caption: Stan Wawrinka waves farewell after his final match in Basel.

sources.originalTitle: Goodbye to the everyman who gatecrashed the greats

segments.body: Wawrinka lost 7-5 7-6 (7-2) to Jiri Lehecka in what proved to be his final tour-level match. The 41-year-old Swiss was in tears with his family and team after the defeat in Basel, where the crowd saw the one-handed backhand and fiery energy that defined his career.

segments.title: A career beyond expectations
segments.body: Wawrinka won the Australian Open in 2014, the French Open in 2015 and the US Open in 2016, beating members of tennis's dominant generation along the way. He said his priority had been to give everything and leave the sport without regrets.

content.headline: Novak Djokovic fights back in Basel to keep ATP Finals hopes alive
content.shortHeadline: Djokovic comeback keeps ATP Finals hopes alive
content.standfirst: Djokovic beat Ugo Humbert in three sets on his return to Basel, where he had not played for 15 years. The 39-year-old remains outside the top eight in the race for the season-ending ATP Finals.

image.caption: Novak Djokovic won the Basel title on his debut at the tournament in 2009.

sources.originalTitle: Djokovic celebrates 'big win' on return to Basel

segments.body: Djokovic recovered from losing the first set to beat France's Ugo Humbert 4-6 6-3 6-4 in two and a half hours. It was his first appearance in Basel since 2011 and his first indoor event since winning the Athens title last November.

The 24-time major winner is 11th in the race to Turin; only the top eight qualify for the ATP Finals. Djokovic called the win "big" and said he had to weather the storm after being under pressure from the start.

content.headline: Rangers rescue a 2-2 draw on Derek McInnes's hostile Hearts return
content.shortHeadline: Rangers rescue draw on McInnes's Hearts return
content.standfirst: A late Olwethu Makhanya header earned Rangers a point at Tynecastle after Hearts fought back from a goal down. The draw capped a heated return for manager Derek McInnes, who left Hearts for Rangers in the summer.

image.caption: Hearts head coach Wouter Vrancken and Rangers manager Derek McInnes exchange a frosty handshake after their 2-2 draw.

sources.originalTitle: Tetchy handshake typifies McInnes' 'topsy-turvy' Tynecastle return

segments.body: Rangers took the lead through Kevin Kelsy, but Hearts rallied and looked set to win before Makhanya's late header made it 2-2. The match was tense on and off the pitch, with Hearts head coach Wouter Vrancken booked before a frosty post-match handshake with McInnes.

McInnes said his side had not controlled a "very topsy-turvy game" and described their performance as below their level. Vrancken said Hearts had deserved to win and praised his depleted squad's fight; he was also unsure how serious an injury to makeshift full-back Rogers Mato might be.

content.headline: Alessia Russo makes Champions League history with Arsenal hat-trick
content.shortHeadline: Russo makes Champions League history with hat-trick
content.standfirst: Russo became England's all-time leading goalscorer in the Women's Champions League as Arsenal beat Benfica 3-0. The result provides a clear standout performance from the latest European matches.

sources.originalTitle: Women's Football

segments.body: Alessia Russo scored all three goals in Arsenal's 3-0 win over Benfica, becoming England's leading goalscorer in the Women's Champions League. The result is among the latest European action highlighted in BBC Sport's women's football coverage.

content.headline: Vincent Kompany leaves hospital after collapse at Bayern training
content.shortHeadline: Kompany discharged from hospital after collapse
content.standfirst: Bayern Munich say their head coach is doing well after being discharged, with the cause of his collapse identified as meningeal irritation. There is still no date for his return to the dugout.

image.caption: Vincent Kompany was appointed Bayern Munich manager in May 2024.

sources.originalTitle: Kompany discharged from hospital following collapse

segments.body: Kompany was taken to hospital after becoming ill while watching Bayern's second team train. Club board member Max Eberl said he had been discharged and was "doing well"; the cause was identified as meningeal irritation, an inflammation of the membrane around the brain and spinal cord.
Bayern have not set a timeline for Kompany's return and previously said it would be a matter of "weeks, not days". Assistant coach Aaron Danks has taken charge in his absence.

content.headline: Benjamin Sesko expected to miss Manchester United games until January
content.shortHeadline: Sesko expected to be out until January
content.standfirst: The Manchester United striker has not played since September and is expected to be sidelined until at least January with a shin injury. His absence leaves the club without its only orthodox number nine.

image.caption: Benjamin Sesko joined Manchester United ahead of the 2025-26 season.

sources.originalTitle: Sesko ruled out until January with shin injury

segments.body: Sesko is expected to be out until at least January after tests on a shin problem that has troubled him since pre-season. The injury is described as an impact injury rather than shin splints. He has not featured since being substituted against Brighton on 16 September.

The 23-year-old has scored twice this season. United are without their only orthodox number nine during a difficult run, with league games against Liverpool and Arsenal among the matches he is expected to miss. The club's next steps are not confirmed.

content.headline: Mikey Lewis aims to help England keep Rugby League World Cup hopes alive
content.shortHeadline: Lewis targets England World Cup lifeline
content.standfirst: After scoring twice in England's 82-0 win over France, Mikey Lewis could again be used from the bench as they try to stay in the Rugby League World Cup. Their route to the semi-finals depends on other results too.

image.caption: Mikey Lewis has scored four tries in nine appearances for England.

sources.originalTitle: 'I earned my spot' - Lewis can be England hero after controversial selection

segments.body: Lewis was left out of England's opening defeat by Tonga but came off the bench to score twice against France. The Hull KR half-back says he earned his place despite an inconsistent season and disciplinary problems, including a four-game ban.

segments.title: Qualification remains uncertain
segments.body: England must beat Papua New Guinea on Friday, hope Tonga defeat Samoa on Sunday and make up a 68-point deficit on Samoa to reach the semi-finals. Lewis is expected to start among the interchanges again; his role and England's progress remain uncertain.
